items.title: Advances in Natural Product Extraction: Established and Emerging Technologies
items.summary: This review examines recent advances in the extraction and isolation of natural products, motivated by the renewed prominence of nature-derived compounds in drug discovery and the recognition that microorganisms, plants, and marine organisms represent an underexplored reservoir of structurally diverse bioactive scaffolds. The authors survey a broad range of established and emerging extraction technologies, including green and designer solvent systems, pressurized and ultrasound-assisted extraction, and supercritical fluid techniques, alongside integrated purification workflows designed to improve compound recovery and reduce processing time. A particular focus is placed on the growing role of artificial intelligence and machine learning in optimizing solvent selection, guiding extraction conditions, and enabling metabolite dereplication within complex biological matrices. The review concludes that combinatorial extraction strategies, next-generation solvent systems, and AI-driven informatic tools have collectively enhanced operational efficiency, selectivity, and analytical throughput in natural product research over the recent period surveyed.
items.citation: Carsyn R. Travis, Jared McMaster, Fatima Rivas. Advances in Natural Product Extraction: Established and Emerging Technologies. Molecules. 2026

items.title: Mining beyond Earth with Space Robots: Exploration, Sampling, and Extraction
items.summary: This paper surveys the field of space mining robotics, examining how autonomous robotic systems can enable the acquisition and utilization of extraterrestrial resources such as helium-3, water, minerals on the Moon and Mars, and asteroid deposits. The authors construct a systematic six-stage architecture spanning exploration, sampling, and extraction, covering activities from remote sensing and in situ detection through single- and multi-robot excavation to autonomous resource extraction and integration into construction or transport pipelines. The review also catalogs existing resources relevant to space mining research, including real-world mission data, terrestrial analog datasets, and simulation environments. The paper further identifies key open challenges facing autonomous space mining and proposes a strategic research roadmap aimed at closing current technological gaps and advancing toward a sustainable off-world economy.
items.citation: Dong Li, Dujun Nie, Xiaotong Zhang et al.. Mining beyond Earth with Space Robots: Exploration, Sampling, and Extraction. arXiv. 2026

items.title: VIALS: A Benchmark for Visual Interpretation of Artifacts in the Life Sciences
items.summary: This paper introduces a benchmark designed to evaluate how well vision-language models can interpret the kinds of visual artifacts that life scientists routinely encounter in professional research settings, such as gel blots, microscopy images, plasmid maps, flow cytometry plots, and molecular structures. The benchmark consists of visual question-answering tasks drawn from realistic biotech industry workflows rather than idealized figures from publications or textbooks. When frontier vision-language models were evaluated on these tasks, they performed poorly, revealing significant gaps in domain-specific knowledge and visual reasoning, even though the same tasks were found to be straightforward for scientists with relevant expertise. The authors argue that this gap has practical consequences, as the ability to interpret such artifacts is central to how life scientists reason, communicate, and make decisions, meaning AI systems that cannot do so will have limited utility in professional life sciences contexts.
items.citation: Elaine Lau, Thanuka Udumulla, Lee Izhaki-Tavor et al.. VIALS: A Benchmark for Visual Interpretation of Artifacts in the Life Sciences. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Magic Velocity Selection in Atom Interferometry
items.summary: The paper investigates a systematic error in atom interferometry that arises from velocity-selective Raman transitions used to prepare atomic ensembles with narrow momentum distributions. Differential light shifts between atomic energy levels create velocity distributions that are spatially correlated with Raman beam intensity, and these inhomogeneous distributions interact with detuning-dependent systematic effects in a Bragg diffraction-based simultaneous conjugate Ramsey-Bordé interferometer. This interaction was found to induce systematic phase shifts on the order of tens of milliradians, representing a significant source of measurement error. The authors identify a "magic" detuning for the velocity selection process at which these correlated systematic phase shifts are suppressed, analogous to magic wavelength techniques used elsewhere in precision measurement. Operating at this magic detuning eliminates errors arising from atom velocity-position correlations, enabling high-precision atom interferometry at sub-part-per-billion accuracy levels.
items.citation: Yuno Iwasaki, Jack Roth, Madeline Bernstein et al.. Magic Velocity Selection in Atom Interferometry. arXiv. 2026

items.title: PerturbRx: Learning Treatment-Conditioned Latent Transitions for Patient Drug Response Prediction
items.summary: PerturbRx is a framework designed to address the challenge of predicting cancer patient drug responses when training data are scarce and tumors are molecularly heterogeneous. Rather than relying solely on pretreatment molecular profiles and drug representations, the approach explicitly models the molecular changes expected to occur under treatment by learning drug- and dose-conditioned transitions in latent space. The transition predictor is trained using context-matched but cell-unpaired control and treated single-cell populations, then transferred to pretreatment patient profiles without requiring post-treatment patient measurements. These learned latent transitions are combined with patient and drug representations to generate response predictions. Evaluated against multiple benchmarks using tumor and patient-derived xenograft data, the framework achieves the strongest aggregate predictive performance among the methods compared, supporting the utility of perturbation-pretrained latent transitions for patient-level drug response prediction.
items.citation: Yoshitaka Inoue, Minoh Jeong, Alfred Hero et al.. PerturbRx: Learning Treatment-Conditioned Latent Transitions for Patient Drug Response Prediction. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Truthful Calibration Measures for Sequential Prediction
items.summary: This paper investigates the theoretical foundations of calibration measures for sequential probabilistic prediction, focusing on the tension between truthfulness, completeness, and soundness. The authors address an open question from prior work about whether exact truthfulness—meaning a forecaster cannot benefit from misreporting probabilities—can coexist with completeness and soundness in a calibration measure. They prove this is impossible for sequential binary prediction, even under independent outcomes, establishing a fundamental incompatibility. To circumvent this impossibility, they develop two general reductions from any base calibration measure that yield approximately truthful variants under additive and multiplicative notions of approximation. Applying the multiplicative reduction, they construct calibration measures that are simultaneously sound, complete, and multiplicatively approximately truthful, improving upon the best previously known guarantees.
items.citation: Anagha Gokul, Jason Hartline, Lunjia Hu et al.. Truthful Calibration Measures for Sequential Prediction. arXiv. 2026

items.title: TurboBias 2.0: Streaming Context-Biasing for Production-Efficient ASR Systems
items.summary: This paper addresses the challenge of incorporating user-provided context phrases into production automatic speech recognition systems that must operate under strict latency and efficiency constraints. The authors developed TurboBias 2.0, a framework for efficient phrase boosting in Transducer-based ASR systems that extends a prior GPU-accelerated approach with case-insensitive boosting graphs and per-stream batched decoding. A key innovation is the ability to assign independent context-biasing configurations to each utterance within a batch, enabling personalized recognition for multiple simultaneous users without mixing their context lists. The framework supports both offline and streaming inference modes and is compatible with greedy and beam-search decoding strategies. Experiments demonstrate that TurboBias 2.0 improves the recognition of contextual phrases while maintaining low latency and high throughput suitable for production deployment.
items.citation: Vladimir Bataev, Lilit Grigoryan, Andrei Andrusenko et al.. TurboBias 2.0: Streaming Context-Biasing for Production-Efficient ASR Systems. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Innovative epitope-based ELISA assay for detecting Group B Streptococcus carriage in pregnant women.
items.summary: This study investigated synthetic peptide epitopes derived from Group B Streptococcus proteins as components for an ELISA-based immunodiagnostic test to detect GBS infection and carriage in pregnant women, addressing limitations of the current culture-based gold standard, which is slow and sometimes ambiguous to interpret. The researchers selected three epitopes from the bacterial proteins GroEL, enolase, and EF-Tu, then tested them individually and in combination against serum samples from GBS-positive and GBS-negative individuals using IgG, IgM, and IgA antibody detection. All three epitopes, whether used alone or mixed, successfully distinguished between GBS-positive and GBS-negative sera, with the enolase-derived and EF-Tu-derived peptides performing best individually due to their higher immunoreactivity at lower concentrations. Combining the epitopes in various mixtures further improved overall immunoreactivity, suggesting a synergistic diagnostic benefit. The authors propose this prototype epitope-based ELISA as a promising and potentially pioneering alternative to conventional GBS diagnostic methods, with no comparable test currently available on the diagnostic market.
items.citation: Brzychczy-Włoch M, Dobrut A, Drożdż K et al.. Innovative epitope-based ELISA assay for detecting Group B Streptococcus carriage in pregnant women.. Applied microbiology and biotechnology. 2026

items.title: Bridging the diagnostic gap: the role of culture methods in the era of syndromic panels for central nervous system infections.
items.summary: This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of a syndromic molecular panel for central nervous system infections by comparing it against conventional culture methods using cerebrospinal fluid samples collected over three years at a national reference center. The researchers assessed concordance, sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values across a large dataset of paired molecular and culture results. The syndromic panel demonstrated high specificity and strong negative predictive value, but its overall sensitivity was limited, partly because the panel's fixed target list excluded clinically relevant pathogens such as certain staphylococcal and streptococcal species as well as rare environmental organisms that conventional culture successfully identified. When the analysis was restricted to only the bacterial targets included in the panel, agreement and sensitivity improved substantially, clarifying that discordance arose largely from the panel's incomplete pathogen coverage rather than analytical failure. The authors conclude that syndromic panels cannot serve as standalone diagnostics and must be systematically combined with conventional culture to ensure comprehensive pathogen detection and guide appropriate antimicrobial therapy, while also calling for next-generation platforms with broader target coverage informed by real-world epidemiology.
items.venue: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
items.citation: Sberna G, D'Arezzo S, Valli MB et al.. Bridging the diagnostic gap: the role of culture methods in the era of syndromic panels for central nervous system infections.. Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology. 2026

items.title: Performance of the LIAISON PLEX gram-positive blood culture assay for identifying bacterial pathogens and resistance genes in blood cultures.
items.summary: This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of the LIAISON PLEX Gram-Positive Blood Culture Assay, a multiplexed molecular test designed to rapidly identify gram-positive bacterial pathogens and antibiotic resistance markers directly from positive blood culture bottles. The researchers conducted a multisite evaluation using a large combination of prospective clinical samples, pre-selected samples, and contrived specimens, assessing the assay's ability to detect and differentiate thirteen gram-positive bacterial targets and four antibiotic resistance markers. The assay demonstrated very high overall sensitivity and specificity across all targets, with a near-perfect valid test rate, and performed well in inclusivity testing, detecting the vast majority of strains tested. Minimal cross-reactivity was observed among off-panel bacterial species, performance was unaffected by common interfering substances, and accuracy was maintained in polymicrobial infection scenarios. The findings support the assay's reliability and accuracy as a rapid diagnostic tool that can inform antibiotic optimization and patient management in the context of gram-positive bloodstream infections.
items.citation: Chow S-K, Stevig C, Granato P et al.. Performance of the LIAISON PLEX gram-positive blood culture assay for identifying bacterial pathogens and resistance genes in blood cultures.. Journal of clinical microbiology. 2026

items.title: Utility and clinical relevance of multiplex PCR panels for diagnosis of central nervous system infections.
items.summary: This study evaluated the real-world diagnostic performance and clinical utility of multiplex polymerase chain reaction panels designed to detect pathogens causing meningitis and encephalitis directly from cerebrospinal fluid. Researchers retrospectively reviewed cerebrospinal fluid samples tested with these panels over a five-year period at a tertiary care hospital, examining test results alongside clinical data and subsequent management decisions. Viral pathogens dominated positive detections, with human herpesvirus-6, enterovirus, and herpes simplex virus type-1 being most frequently identified, while Streptococcus pneumoniae was the leading bacterial finding, and co-detections occurred in a notable proportion of positive cases. Despite the panels' capacity for rapid pathogen identification, fewer than half of positive results led to a clinically relevant change in diagnosis or treatment, and repeat testing after an initial negative result yielded little additional diagnostic benefit. The authors conclude that inappropriate test utilisation and gaps in clinician awareness about panel content limit the clinical impact of these tools, and that clearer testing criteria are needed to improve diagnostic efficiency.
items.venue: The Indian journal of medical research
items.citation: Gürler M, Karaoğlu Ç, Yurtcu EE et al.. Utility and clinical relevance of multiplex PCR panels for diagnosis of central nervous system infections.. The Indian journal of medical research. 2026

items.title: Validation of an in-house developed rapid assay for Group B Streptococcus detection in pregnancy.
items.summary: This study addressed the need for rapid, accurate detection of Group B Streptococcus colonization in pregnant women, a key risk factor for neonatal infections and preterm stillbirth. The researchers developed an in-house assay combining CRISPR/Cas12a with recombinase polymerase amplification, an isothermal amplification method, to create a platform that could be read visually via colloidal gold test strips or through a fluorescence reader. Specificity was tested against multiple reproductive tract pathogens, and sensitivity was established using gradient-diluted plasmid standards, while clinical validation employed vaginal-rectal swabs from pregnant women benchmarked against commercial quantitative real-time PCR. The assay completed detection within one hour, accurately distinguished Group B Streptococcus from non-target pathogens, and showed close agreement with conventional PCR results across a large clinical sample set. The authors conclude that this rapid platform demonstrates high sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy, suggesting strong potential for clinical use in prenatal screening settings.
items.venue: International journal of medical microbiology : IJMM
items.citation: Hu S, Xie J, Liu L et al.. Validation of an in-house developed rapid assay for Group B Streptococcus detection in pregnancy.. International journal of medical microbiology : IJMM. 2026

items.title: Advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarkers, 2020-26: scientific evidence, recommendations, gaps, and developmental priorities.
items.summary: This review examines major advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarker research over roughly a five-year period, synthesizing evidence that has informed updated WHO policy guidance consolidating recommendations for detecting tuberculosis disease and drug resistance into a single framework. Digital chest radiography supported by computer-aided detection has been established as a core screening and triage tool, while decentralised molecular diagnosis has expanded through multiple classes of rapid nucleic acid amplification tests, novel specimen types such as tongue swabs, and workflow innovations including sputum pooling. Diagnostic accuracy in children and sputum-scarce populations has improved through extended use of non-sputum specimens, and targeted next-generation sequencing has been recognised for comprehensive drug-susceptibility testing at reference laboratory level. Host blood transcriptomic and other biomarker signatures show promising triage and prognostic performance, yet no biomarker has met WHO target product profile criteria for a point-of-care test capable of reliably distinguishing infection from active disease, including subclinical tuberculosis. The authors conclude that substantial gaps in performance, implementation, and equity remain, underscoring continued developmental priorities in this field.
items.citation: Walzl G, McHugh TD, Chakaya J et al.. Advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarkers, 2020-26: scientific evidence, recommendations, gaps, and developmental priorities.. The Lancet. Microbe. 2027

items.title: Development of a microfluidic isothermal amplification nucleic acid detection (mFIND) platform for simultaneous detection of respiratory pathogens.
items.summary: The paper describes the development of a centrifugal microfluidic platform designed to simultaneously detect multiple respiratory pathogens—influenza A and B, SARS-CoV-2, and RSV—at the point of care. The system integrates lyophilized reagents into independent reaction chambers on a microfluidic chip, uses isothermal amplification at a fixed temperature, and employs real-time fluorescence monitoring, all automated within a portable analyzer. The platform achieves extremely low limits of detection with no cross-reactivity against a broad panel of non-target pathogens, and clinical validation against a large set of positive samples demonstrated complete agreement with conventional quantitative PCR. The entire detection process is completed within fifteen minutes using very small reaction volumes, making it suitable for decentralized or resource-limited settings. The authors position this platform as a practical nucleic acid testing solution capable of processing multiple targets in parallel with a simplified workflow and room-temperature reagent storage.
items.citation: He P, Feng Y, Zhou X et al.. Development of a microfluidic isothermal amplification nucleic acid detection (mFIND) platform for simultaneous detection of respiratory pathogens.. Biosensors & bioelectronics. 2026

items.title: Development and evaluation of a rapid duplex qPCR assay for Treponema pallidum using the GeneSoC microfluidic platform.
items.summary: This paper studied the development and evaluation of a rapid molecular diagnostic assay for detecting Treponema pallidum, the causative agent of syphilis, with point-of-care applications in mind. The researchers designed a duplex quantitative PCR assay targeting two genomic regions and implemented it on a microfluidic platform, testing it against DNA standards, a reference strain, and clinical specimens including lesion swabs and urine, with and without prior DNA extraction. The assay demonstrated good linearity and amplification efficiency across both targets, showed no cross-reactivity with other pathogens, and achieved qualitative agreement with a conventional comparator assay. Notably, the microfluidic platform completed detection within fifteen minutes, substantially faster than the comparator system, and successfully detected the pathogen in a specimen collected during the seronegative window period. The authors conclude that the assay is suitable for rapid clinical detection directly from specimens without DNA extraction, though extraction may benefit samples with low pathogen burden.
items.citation: Kawahata T, Banno F, Hama M. Development and evaluation of a rapid duplex qPCR assay for Treponema pallidum using the GeneSoC microfluidic platform.. Diagnostic microbiology and infectious disease. 2026

items.title: Trends of nucleic acid - based point-of-care diagnostics for infectious diseases.
items.summary: This review examines the current landscape of nucleic acid-based point-of-care diagnostics for infectious diseases, motivated by the global need for decentralized, rapid, and accessible testing. The authors survey the full diagnostic workflow across three operational stages: nucleic acid extraction, amplification, and detection, covering platforms such as lateral flow assays, biochips, and biosensors. For extraction, they assess approaches including magnetic bead-based, paper-based, and integrated microfluidic methods, emphasizing designs that are simplified and equipment-free. Amplification strategies reviewed include both thermal cycling methods like PCR and isothermal alternatives such as LAMP, RPA, and NASBA, all adapted for portable and low-power conditions. On the detection side, the review spans colorimetric and fluorescent assays through to advanced programmable biosensors exploiting CRISPR/Cas systems and toehold switch mechanisms, highlighting their potential for highly sensitive and selective nucleic acid recognition outside conventional laboratory settings.
items.citation: Hatem H, Mysara M, Ramadan R. Trends of nucleic acid - based point-of-care diagnostics for infectious diseases.. Journal of biological engineering. 2026

items.title: A nested PCR-based point-of-care multiplex test for detection of bacterial pathogens in cerebrospinal fluids.
items.summary: This study developed and evaluated a multiplex one-tube nested real-time PCR assay integrated with a point-of-care testing instrument for detecting three bacterial pathogens — *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Streptococcus agalactiae*, and *Streptococcus pyogenes* — directly from cerebrospinal fluid samples. The method was designed to automate the entire workflow from sample input to result output, combining fully automated nucleic acid extraction with highly sensitive nested PCR chemistry. The assay demonstrated very low detection limits with no cross-reactivity against other common pathogens, and reduced total testing time compared to manual extraction paired with conventional real-time PCR. When evaluated against clinical cerebrospinal fluid and non-CSF samples, the point-of-care system identified additional positive cases that conventional real-time PCR had missed, indicating superior sensitivity. The authors conclude that this integrated approach offers a rapid, culture-free, and operationally streamlined solution for diagnosing bacterial central nervous system infections at the point of care.
items.venue: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
items.citation: Wu J, Zhao Z, Pang P et al.. A nested PCR-based point-of-care multiplex test for detection of bacterial pathogens in cerebrospinal fluids.. Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology. 2026

items.title: A Novel Voltammetric Point-of-Care Device for Rapid and Accurate Nucleic Acid and Viral Pathogen Detection.
items.summary: This paper developed and evaluated a novel electrochemical nucleic acid amplification test that combines isothermal amplification with real-time voltammetric detection for diagnosing viral pathogens. The approach detects protons released during amplification by monitoring pH changes through a redox-active sensing compound, offering an alternative to optical detection methods that can hamper conventional isothermal techniques like LAMP. The system was tested against multiple respiratory viruses including SARS-CoV-2, influenza A and B viruses, and RSV A using RNA purified from clinical samples, achieving high concordance with the gold-standard RT-qPCR method. A proof-of-concept extraction-free workflow was also demonstrated using equine nasal swab samples tested for a horse herpesvirus, with all samples correctly classified relative to quantitative PCR. The authors conclude that real-time voltammetric LAMP is feasible across several sample types and pathogens, while acknowledging that broader validation in additional matrices and prospective cohorts is still needed.
items.citation: Munita R, Lyttleton R, Danefur E et al.. A Novel Voltammetric Point-of-Care Device for Rapid and Accurate Nucleic Acid and Viral Pathogen Detection.. ACS omega. 2026

items.title: Biosensing technologies for foodborne pathogen detection and healthcare: principles, emerging materials, and intelligent platforms
items.summary: This review examines the current state and future directions of biosensing technologies designed to detect high-priority foodborne pathogens, including Escherichia coli, Salmonella, and Listeria monocytogenes, which continue to threaten global public health. The authors survey electrochemical, optical, and microfluidic sensing platforms, assessing how advances in functional nanomaterials, aptamers, nanozymes, and surface engineering have improved sensor sensitivity, specificity, and performance in complex food matrices. A central theme is the integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning into biosensor systems, which enables real-time analytics, pattern recognition, and high-throughput multiplexed detection, effectively transforming conventional detection tools into intelligent diagnostic devices. The review critically evaluates biosensor design principles, signal transduction mechanisms, and performance validation while identifying key challenges such as matrix interference, bioreceptor instability, scalability limitations, and the absence of regulatory standardization, alongside mitigation strategies including ratiometric sensing, microfluidic pre-treatment, and explainable AI. Looking ahead, the authors advocate for self-powered biosensors, modular pathogen detection panels, blockchain-based data integrity, and standardized validation pipelines as pathways toward regulation-ready platforms for next-generation food safety monitoring.
items.citation: Purshottam J. Assudani, Balakrishnan . P., Anny Leema A et al.. Biosensing technologies for foodborne pathogen detection and healthcare: principles, emerging materials, and intelligent platforms. Microchimica Acta. 2026

items.title: Data-Centric Foundation Models in Computational Healthcare: A Survey
items.summary: This survey examines the intersection of foundation models and computational healthcare through a data-centric lens, focusing on how data quality, quantity, and characterization shape AI performance in clinical settings. The authors reviewed a broad range of data-centric approaches spanning the full lifecycle of foundation models, from pre-training through inference, as applied to healthcare workflows. Key challenges addressed include obtaining high-quality clinical data, handling annotation burdens, protecting patient privacy, and navigating ethical considerations. The survey also discusses AI security, model assessment, and alignment with human values as critical dimensions of deploying foundation models responsibly in medicine. The authors conclude with an outlook suggesting that data-centric foundation model analytics hold significant promise for improving patient outcomes and streamlining clinical workflows.
items.citation: Yunkun Zhang, Jin Gao, Zheling Tan et al.. Data-Centric Foundation Models in Computational Healthcare: A Survey. ACM Computing Surveys. 2026

items.title: Comprehensive Review on Candidemia: Epidemiology, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Future Directions
items.summary: This review examines candidemia, a serious bloodstream infection caused by *Candida* species that represents a major source of hospital-acquired illness with high mortality and significant healthcare burden. The authors synthesize current knowledge spanning the epidemiology, species distribution, and origins of candidemia, alongside a critical appraisal of existing diagnostic methods and their shortcomings, particularly the delays introduced by conventional detection approaches. The review evaluates both empiric and targeted antifungal treatment strategies, addressing mixed infections, host-drug interactions, antifungal resistance, and the potential role of combination therapy in overcoming resistance. Emerging diagnostic technologies and novel antifungal agents currently in clinical development, including compounds directed at new fungal pathway targets, are also assessed. Looking forward, the review highlights the potential of artificial intelligence in diagnostics, vaccine-based prophylaxis, and synergistic therapeutic strategies as promising directions for improving patient outcomes in candidemia management.
items.citation: Haojie Dong, Minghui Song, Jingfang Sun et al.. Comprehensive Review on Candidemia: Epidemiology, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Future Directions. iFungi. 2026

items.title: Multi-omics and artificial intelligence for precision drug discovery and potential clinical applications
items.summary: This review examines how the integration of multiomics technologies with artificial intelligence is reshaping precision drug discovery and clinical medicine. The authors synthesize current knowledge on how genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic approaches, when combined with deep learning architectures, can decode complex molecular datasets to reveal disease mechanisms and biological patterns. The review covers the application of this combined framework across the drug development pipeline, including target identification, drug repositioning, de novo compound design, virtual screening, pharmacokinetic modeling, and safety assessment. Disease areas such as oncology, neurodegeneration, and cardiovascular conditions are used to illustrate the practical potential of these converging technologies. The authors acknowledge persistent challenges including harmonization of heterogeneous data streams, reproducibility concerns, and algorithmic bias, while arguing that the fusion of multiomics and artificial intelligence opens a new era of data-driven, bench-to-clinic translational medicine.
items.citation: Yuqing Liu, Kun Zhu, Weijun Peng et al.. Multi-omics and artificial intelligence for precision drug discovery and potential clinical applications. Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. 2026

items.title: Natural-Language Workflows Are Not Software Yet: Artifact-Driven Compilation for Reliable Agent Execution
items.summary: This paper addresses the problem of agents unreliably executing natural-language workflows, which often leave data dependencies implicit and contain branching logic that overburdens language model executors. The authors propose Artic, a compiler that transforms natural-language workflows into a structured artifact-driven representation where each step explicitly declares the artifacts it reads and writes, constraints gate produced artifacts, and control flow is made explicit. The compiler identifies steps that place excessive demands on agent execution and refines them through constrained optimization, then validates the transformation by decomposing faithfulness checking into local obligations and using scenario-based dry runs to verify conformance with the source workflow. Evaluated across a large set of problem instances drawn from real-world domain workflows, Artic substantially improves task resolution rates compared to executing the original text workflows. The compiled workflows also show markedly greater consistency when evaluated across different models and in repeated executions of the same workflow.
items.citation: Xiangzhe Xu, Hanxi Guo, Guangyu Shen et al.. Natural-Language Workflows Are Not Software Yet: Artifact-Driven Compilation for Reliable Agent Execution. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Anatomy-Informed Neural Networks: Encoding Anatomic Priors in Loss and Architecture, with an SE(3) Formulation of Guidewire-Induced Aortoiliac Deformation
items.summary: This paper introduces Anatomy-Informed Neural Networks (AINN), a framework that encodes anatomical knowledge into deep learning models either as soft penalty terms in the loss function or as hard constraints built directly into the network architecture, analogous to how physics-informed neural networks incorporate physical laws. The approach is developed around the clinical problem of predicting how the aortoiliac vasculature deforms when a stiff guidewire is inserted endoluminally, a scenario relevant to aortic surgery and autonomous endovascular navigation. The vessel centerline and wire path are represented as curves of frames in the Lie group SE(3), coupling a Cosserat-rod model of the wire to the vessel through a contact inequality constraint, with the deformation predicted as a constrained minimizer of coupled elastic energy. Training supervision uses a Wasserstein-2 optimal-transport loss between predicted angiographic projections and observed two-dimensional angiograms, enabling three-dimensional predictions from two-dimensional imaging. The current work is fully in silico with no network yet trained, serving as a verified computational foundation for future transfer to real clinical data.
items.citation: David P. Stonko. Anatomy-Informed Neural Networks: Encoding Anatomic Priors in Loss and Architecture, with an SE(3) Formulation of Guidewire-Induced Aortoiliac Deformation. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Time-Aware Tranformer-Based Prediction Model for AECOPD
items.summary: The paper addresses the challenge of predicting acute exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD) in a timely manner, noting that conventional approaches relying on clinical and laboratory data introduce problematic delays. To overcome this limitation, the authors focused on home monitoring scenarios using only respiratory data collected from daily-use ventilators. They developed a Time-Aware transformer-based model capable of capturing both symptom patterns and their temporal progression within the ventilator data, generating meaningful patient representations without requiring clinical inputs. Experimental results showed that the proposed model outperformed traditional machine learning methods across multiple classification tasks, suggesting it could improve both the speed and accuracy of AECOPD prediction in real-world home settings.
items.citation: Weihao Qu, Ling Zheng, Dongyang Wang et al.. Time-Aware Tranformer-Based Prediction Model for AECOPD. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Hypothesis testing between quantum ensembles
items.summary: This paper studies the problem of distinguishing between two quantum state ensembles using hypothesis testing, extending classical binary hypothesis testing to the setting where each observation consists of a quantum state accompanied by a classical label. The authors formulate the discrimination task by recognizing that ensembles are invariant under label permutations, which distinguishes them from classical-quantum states, and they characterize the joint sampled state through power-weighted ensemble moments. From this framework, they derive the Bayes-optimal measurement and exact finite-sample error probabilities, showing that discrimination depends on the full hierarchy of ensemble moments up to the number of samples taken. In the many-sample regime, they establish Chernoff bounds and exact error exponents for finite uniform pure-state ensembles. Applying these results to optical communication and quantum designs, they find that for pure-state designs with large design parameter, the maximal discrimination exponent decreases sharply with that parameter while the number of samples required for reliable discrimination grows correspondingly, revealing a fundamental trade-off between the complexity of the ensemble and the difficulty of distinguishing it from alternatives.
items.citation: Jian Yao, Quntao Zhuang. Hypothesis testing between quantum ensembles. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Rethinking Expressivity and Efficiency in Test-Time Training
items.summary: The paper addresses a fundamental tension in Test-Time Training (TTT) methods for long-context sequence processing, where per-token weight update dynamics offer expressivity but are computationally expensive, while chunk-wise approximations are efficient but lose important temporal structure. The authors propose a method that derives a closed-form state transition under standard chunk-start weight approximations, allowing exact reproduction of per-token fast-weight and momentum states at chunk boundaries without sacrificing parallelization. This approach preserves the temporal structure of update rules that prior chunk-wise methods discard, enabling fully parallelized training while remaining expressive. Models trained with this method perform comparably to existing TTT and hybrid attention baselines on language modeling and surpass them on in-context retrieval, with particularly strong gains in length extrapolation, retaining high accuracy on a passkey retrieval benchmark at context lengths far beyond those seen during training. The method also matches the training throughput of efficient chunk-wise approaches, demonstrating that expressivity and hardware efficiency need not be in conflict.
items.citation: Zeyun Zhong, Joya Chen, Manuel Martin et al.. Rethinking Expressivity and Efficiency in Test-Time Training. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Basin-Preserving Discretizations of Modern Hopfield Retrieval Dynamics: Energy Cells, Dissipation, and the Attention Limit
items.summary: This paper investigates which numerical time-discretization schemes for modern Hopfield network retrieval dynamics faithfully preserve not just energy decay and fixed points, but also the basins of attraction of stored patterns. The authors introduce the concept of "energy cells," defined as connected components of sublevel sets that contain exactly one attractor and no other critical point, and prove that these cells are simultaneously preserved by the continuous gradient flow, relaxed attention maps with relaxation parameters in a specified range, and implicit Euler methods within their uniqueness regime. A parameter-uniform majorant is constructed to guarantee unconditional energy dissipation and monotone interpolation of discrete steps, while explicit local contraction bounds near well-separated patterns identify a certified optimal slight overrelaxation. The study also characterizes failure modes such as proximal tunneling and overshoot outside the preservation regimes, establishes an order barrier for scalar reparametrizations of the relaxed family, constructs a second-order scalar-auxiliary-variable scheme, and extends the basin-preservation results to damped difference-of-convex iterations in Bregman geometry. Numerical experiments in two dimensions confirm the theoretical bounds, finding that all observed disagreements between continuous and discrete retrieval occur above the attractor-specific inferred escape energy level.
items.citation: Francisco R. Villatoro. Basin-Preserving Discretizations of Modern Hopfield Retrieval Dynamics: Energy Cells, Dissipation, and the Attention Limit. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Respiratory multi-viral rapid-antigen point-of-care tests in New Zealand primary care: a mixed-methods pilot.
items.summary: This study investigated whether multi-viral rapid-antigen point-of-care tests for acute respiratory infections could be feasibly integrated into routine primary care in New Zealand, and examined how patients and clinicians responded to their use. Conducted as a prospective mixed-methods pilot across seven primary care clinics during winter, the study enrolled patients presenting with acute respiratory symptoms and assessed outcomes through medical record audits, surveys, and qualitative interviews and focus groups. A demographically diverse cohort was tested, with a minority returning positive results for any respiratory virus. Both clinicians and patients reported high acceptability of the tests, with all clinicians finding the results useful in practice; a substantial proportion of prescribers indicated that test results influenced their antibiotic prescribing decisions, and a smaller proportion used results to guide secondary care referrals. The authors conclude that these tests were readily incorporated into primary care workflows and suggest that routine integration could improve management of common respiratory illnesses while also encouraging patients who test positive to adopt behaviours that reduce viral transmission.
items.citation: Bibby S, Marsh S, Dowell A et al.. Respiratory multi-viral rapid-antigen point-of-care tests in New Zealand primary care: a mixed-methods pilot.. BJGP open. 2026

items.title: Evaluation of the QuickFinder COVID-19/Flu/RSV antigen test for rapid simultaneous detection of SARS-CoV-2, influenza A/B viruses, and respiratory syncytial virus.
items.summary: This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of a lateral flow immunoassay-based antigen rapid diagnostic test designed to simultaneously detect SARS-CoV-2, influenza A, influenza B, and respiratory syncytial virus from nasopharyngeal swab specimens. Archived specimens were tested in parallel using this rapid test and real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction as the reference standard, with cross-reactivity also assessed against a panel of respiratory pathogens. The rapid test demonstrated high sensitivity for SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A, somewhat lower sensitivity for influenza B and RSV, and perfect specificity for all four targets, with no cross-reactivity observed. Sensitivity was consistently strong in specimens with high viral loads but declined in low viral load samples. The authors conclude that the test is a reliable rapid screening tool for major respiratory viruses but should complement rather than replace molecular testing, particularly when viral loads are low.
items.citation: Kim JA, Kang M, Yu HJ et al.. Evaluation of the QuickFinder COVID-19/Flu/RSV antigen test for rapid simultaneous detection of SARS-CoV-2, influenza A/B viruses, and respiratory syncytial virus.. Diagnostic microbiology and infectious disease. 2026

items.title: No detection of respiratory syncytial virus at one clinic in Japan with rapid immunochromatographic antigen tests for three viruses using the same nasopharyngeal swabs from adult patients
items.summary: This study examined the burden of respiratory syncytial virus infection among adult patients at a Japanese clinic by testing nasopharyngeal swabs collected from adults presenting with acute respiratory infection symptoms. Samples were analyzed using rapid immunochromatographic antigen tests capable of simultaneously detecting SARS-CoV-2, influenza A and B viruses, and RSV. While numerous patients tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A, and one for influenza B, no RSV-positive cases were identified. Comparing these findings against previous reports that used polymerase chain reaction testing revealed a statistically significant difference in RSV detection rates, suggesting that rapid immunochromatographic antigen tests have limited diagnostic utility for identifying RSV infections in Japanese adults compared to PCR-based approaches.
items.citation: Kajiwara N, Tsunetoshi Y, Shiode S. No detection of respiratory syncytial virus at one clinic in Japan with rapid immunochromatographic antigen tests for three viruses using the same nasopharyngeal swabs from adult patients. 2026

items.title: Performance of an antigen test for detection of SARS-CoV-2, influenza, and respiratory syncytial virus-a prospective study.
items.summary: This prospective study evaluated the diagnostic performance of a multiplex rapid antigen test capable of simultaneously detecting SARS-CoV-2, influenza A, influenza B, and respiratory syncytial virus in patients presenting with acute respiratory infection symptoms. The study enrolled over a thousand symptomatic patients, including children, comparing results from a nasal swab antigen test interpreted by emergency department staff against PCR performed on separately collected nasopharyngeal samples at a central laboratory. Sensitivity for each pathogen was assessed at different PCR cycle threshold levels to gauge the test's utility as a marker of infectiousness rather than simply a diagnostic tool. The test demonstrated high sensitivity for all four viruses when using a cycle threshold cutoff associated with meaningful viral load, and achieved perfect specificity across all pathogens and age groups. The findings also revealed that nasal swabs absorbed less viral RNA than nasopharyngeal swabs, particularly for influenza A, though this difference was not observed in children, and the authors conclude the test has potential utility as an infectiousness marker in acute clinical care settings.

items.title: Respiratory Viral Burden and Healthcare Utilization Among Pediatric Patients With Acute Respiratory Viral Infections in a Tertiary Care Center.
items.summary: This study examined the clinical and epidemiological burden of respiratory viral infections, particularly RSV and influenza, in pediatric patients presenting to a tertiary care emergency department in Saudi Arabia during the winter season. Using a retrospective cohort design, researchers tested patients across all age groups with a rapid antigen panel detecting multiple respiratory pathogens, then analyzed clinical outcomes and healthcare resource utilization within the pediatric subgroup. RSV and Influenza A were the predominant pathogens identified, with peak positivity occurring in January and burden concentrated heavily among children under five years of age. A substantial proportion of infected children required hospitalization and advanced respiratory support including high-flow nasal cannula and non-invasive ventilation, though ICU admissions remained infrequent. The authors conclude that seasonal RSV and influenza infections place considerable strain on pediatric emergency and inpatient services, underscoring the need for proactive resource allocation and preventive strategies to manage winter respiratory illness peaks.
items.citation: Alsharif S. Respiratory Viral Burden and Healthcare Utilization Among Pediatric Patients With Acute Respiratory Viral Infections in a Tertiary Care Center.. Health science reports. 2026

items.title: Can exercise affect immune function to increase susceptibility to infection?
items.summary: This debate paper examined the longstanding question in exercise immunology of whether exercise itself can suppress immune function and increase susceptibility to infection. The authors structured opposing arguments around four contested issues: whether athletes are genuinely more infection-prone than the general population, whether exercise independently alters immunity beyond confounding factors such as sleep disruption, travel, anxiety, and nutritional deficits, whether commonly used biomarkers reliably reflect immune health in those performing arduous exercise, and whether the existing scientific evidence is sufficient to support claims about exercise-induced immunosuppression. A broad consensus exists that regular moderate-intensity exercise of shorter duration is beneficial for immune defense, particularly in older and chronically ill individuals, while high-volume arduous exercise practiced by elite athletes and military personnel has long been associated with elevated infection burden. The debating groups agreed that infection susceptibility is multifactorial in origin, but could not resolve whether exercise per se is a direct causative factor of increased infection risk independent of the many lifestyle and environmental stressors that accompany intense training. The authors conclude that the question remains open and call for more rigorous empirical research to disentangle exercise's specific contribution to infection susceptibility from these numerous confounding variables.
items.citation: Richard J. Simpson, Richard J. Simpson, Maree Gleeson et al.. Can exercise affect immune function to increase susceptibility to infection?. PubMed. 2026

items.title: Spinal cord injury: Known and possible influences on the immune response to exercise
items.summary: This review paper examined how spinal cord injury affects immune function, with particular focus on the immune response to exercise. The authors conducted a comprehensive literature search to synthesize existing research on exercise immunology across patient, recreationally active, and athlete populations with spinal cord injury. A central theme is that loss of autonomic function following spinal cord injury alters resting and post-exercise catecholamine concentrations, which directly affects lymphoid cells that express adrenergic receptors, thereby depressing immunity. However, the review also identifies exceptions to this pattern, such as preserved mucosal immune responses to exercise and increased natural killer cell cytotoxicity in individuals with tetraplegia that appear independent of catecholamine changes, suggesting compensatory mechanisms involving sympathetic reflex activity, receptor hypersensitivity, or neuroendocrine adjustments may offset some deficits. The authors conclude that exercise and rehabilitation can improve certain immune and autonomic measures in this population, and call for further research to clarify the mechanisms underlying the immune response to exercise in spinal cord injury to better inform strategies for maintaining health.
items.citation: Christof A. Leicht, Victoria L. Goosey‐Tolfrey, Nicolette C. Bishop. Spinal cord injury: Known and possible influences on the immune response to exercise. PubMed. 2026

items.title: Understanding graft-versus-host disease. Preliminary findings regarding the effects of exercise in affected patients
items.summary: This paper examines graft-versus-host disease, a serious complication arising when donor lymphocytes attack host tissues following allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, with particular attention to its chronic form and the resulting burden on patients' physical capacity. The authors conducted a review of the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying the disease alongside available evidence from both animal and human studies on the effects of exercise as an adjunct therapy. Their findings suggest that exercise training holds promise for improving physical fitness and potentially immune function while reducing fatigue in affected patients, though the evidence base remains limited. The authors conclude that more randomized controlled trials specifically targeting this patient population are needed before firm clinical recommendations can be made.
items.citation: Carmen Fiuza‐Luces, Nuria Garatachea, Nathan A. Berger et al.. Understanding graft-versus-host disease. Preliminary findings regarding the effects of exercise in affected patients. PubMed. 2026

items.title: Disorders of Gut–Brain Interaction and the Rome V Process
items.summary: This paper describes the development and scope of the Rome V criteria for disorders of gut–brain interaction, which are gastrointestinal conditions arising from disturbances in motility, visceral sensitivity, mucosal function, gut microbiota, or central nervous system processing. The Rome Foundation undertook a comprehensive update of the field's knowledge accumulated since the previous Rome IV criteria were published, with an emphasis on evidence-based refinements. The resulting framework revises diagnostic definitions, incorporates new understanding of diet, the gut microenvironment, pharmacogenomics, and biopsychosocial and cross-cultural factors, and updates both diagnostic algorithms and therapeutic approaches. The process also aimed to improve clinical and research language by reducing imprecise or stigmatizing terminology and by integrating patient illness experience and sociocultural perspectives into the criteria.
items.citation: Douglas A. Drossman, L Chang, Jan Tack. Disorders of Gut–Brain Interaction and the Rome V Process. Gastroenterology. 2026

items.title: Osteoarthritis: molecular pathogenesis and potential therapeutic options
items.summary: This review paper examines the molecular pathogenesis of osteoarthritis, a chronic joint disorder characterized by pain, inflammation, and bone deterioration, with a focus on identifying therapeutic targets that current treatments fail to adequately address. The authors synthesize recent findings on nociceptive pathways connecting the knee joint to the central nervous system, inflammatory mediator activity, and organelle-level dysfunctions including mitochondrial impairment, lysosomal destabilization, and unresolved endoplasmic reticulum stress, all of which drive cartilage degradation and disease progression. By integrating these mechanistic insights, the review proposes a multimodal therapeutic framework that simultaneously targets inflammatory cascades, restores organelle homeostasis through strategies such as mitophagy enhancement and lysosomal integrity preservation, and attenuates pain signaling. The authors also highlight organelle-targeted drug delivery systems as a means to improve therapeutic efficacy and stability. Collectively, the review presents these converging insights as a foundation for developing more effective interventions against both the structural and symptomatic dimensions of osteoarthritis.
items.citation: Yi Zhang, Yanqi Han, Ying Sun et al.. Osteoarthritis: molecular pathogenesis and potential therapeutic options. Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. 2026

items.title: Advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarkers, 2020-26: scientific evidence, recommendations, gaps, and developmental priorities.
items.summary: This paper reviews major advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarker research over a five-year period, synthesizing findings that have informed updated WHO policy guidance consolidating recommendations for detecting tuberculosis disease and drug resistance. The authors examined progress across screening tools, molecular diagnostic platforms, specimen types, and biomarker development, noting that digital chest radiography with computer-aided detection has become a core recommended screening tool, while decentralised molecular testing has expanded through multiple classes of nucleic acid amplification tests and novel specimen types such as tongue swabs and stool samples. Drug-resistance testing has been strengthened by new molecular assays and the endorsement of targeted next-generation sequencing at reference laboratory level, and urine-based lipoarabinomannan assays offer diagnostic benefit specifically in people with HIV and advanced disease. Host blood transcriptomic and other biomarker signatures show promise for prognosis and triage, yet no biomarker has met WHO target product profile criteria for a point-of-care test capable of reliably distinguishing infection from disease, including subclinical forms. The paper concludes that meaningful performance, implementation, and equity gaps persist despite these advances.
items.citation: Walzl G, McHugh TD, Chakaya J et al.. Advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarkers, 2020-26: scientific evidence, recommendations, gaps, and developmental priorities.. The Lancet. Microbe. 2027

items.title: SARS-CoV-2 Point-of-Care Testing Modalities: Integrating Molecular, Immunological, Biosensor, and AI Approaches.
items.summary: This review examined the landscape of point-of-care testing technologies for SARS-CoV-2, motivated by the diagnostic demands exposed by the COVID-19 pandemic. The authors conducted a structured literature search across major scientific databases and evaluated molecular assays, antigen and antibody tests, biosensor platforms, and artificial intelligence-assisted diagnostic approaches. Molecular methods such as rapid RT-PCR, LAMP, and CRISPR-based technologies were found to offer high sensitivity and specificity suited for decentralized use, while antigen tests provide rapid and affordable screening with performance that varies by viral load and circulating variant. Antibody-based testing was deemed more appropriate for seroprevalence and immune monitoring than acute infection detection, and biosensor and AI-enabled systems showed promise but remain largely at prototype or early-validation stages. The review concludes that no single modality is universally optimal, and that complementary use of these approaches, alongside advances in multiplexing and variant-resilient design, is needed to strengthen both COVID-19 management and future pandemic preparedness.
items.citation: Hetta HF, Ahmed R, Haseeb A et al.. SARS-CoV-2 Point-of-Care Testing Modalities: Integrating Molecular, Immunological, Biosensor, and AI Approaches.. Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland). 2026

items.title: AI-Enhanced Point-of-Care Diagnostics for Infectious Diseases in Resource-Limited Settings: A Scoping Review.
items.summary: This scoping review systematically mapped research on artificial intelligence-enhanced point-of-care and rapid diagnostic technologies for infectious diseases in resource-limited settings, examining the breadth, nature, and methodological quality of published studies. Following established scoping review methodology, the authors searched five major databases spanning roughly a decade of literature, screening over a thousand records and ultimately including more than two hundred studies. The field was found to be growing rapidly, dominated by work on a narrow triad of diseases and by deep learning approaches such as convolutional neural networks, while neglected tropical diseases remained substantially underrepresented. A critical finding was that prospective field validation was reported in only a small fraction of studies, and geographic coverage was skewed toward East Africa and South Asia, leaving West Africa and Latin America largely absent. The authors conclude that despite rapid growth, the field has serious gaps in validation rigour, disease equity, and geographic inclusivity, and they call for studies that prioritize real-world field testing and engage end-user communities from the outset of research design.
items.venue: Tropical medicine & international health : TM & IH
items.citation: Farquhar H. AI-Enhanced Point-of-Care Diagnostics for Infectious Diseases in Resource-Limited Settings: A Scoping Review.. Tropical medicine & international health : TM & IH. 2026

items.title: An integrated centrifugal microfluidic CRISPR-based diagnostics platform for multiplexed point-of-care testing of respiratory pathogens.
items.summary: The paper developed and validated the iCARD platform, an integrated centrifugal microfluidic diagnostic system designed for multiplexed point-of-care detection of respiratory pathogens. The platform combines a pre-loaded lyophilized CRISPR/Cas13a disc with a portable fluorescence analyzer and a novel resin-based nucleic acid purification method, enabling automated processing of throat swab samples without complex manual steps. The system can simultaneously screen six respiratory pathogens across four independent samples in under an hour, achieving single-copy analytical sensitivity with no cross-reactivity observed. Clinical validation using retrospective patient samples demonstrated near-perfect diagnostic sensitivity and complete specificity, confirming the platform's accuracy. The authors conclude that iCARD represents a robust and practical tool for decentralized molecular diagnostics and epidemiological surveillance.
items.citation: Li L, Wei H, Wei M et al.. An integrated centrifugal microfluidic CRISPR-based diagnostics platform for multiplexed point-of-care testing of respiratory pathogens.. Biosensors & bioelectronics. 2026

items.title: Point-of-care testing (POCT) for Infectious diseases: technological innovation, effectiveness evaluation, and application strategies in resource-limited regions.
items.summary: This review paper examines point-of-care testing technologies for infectious diseases, with particular focus on their relevance for early screening, epidemic surveillance, and public health prevention. The authors systematically surveyed recent advances across molecular diagnostics, microfluidic systems, biosensing technologies, and artificial intelligence as applied to rapid diagnostic tools. They also analyzed the quality assessment frameworks used to evaluate these technologies, including measures of sensitivity, specificity, detection limits, stability, and field suitability. Special consideration was given to deployment strategies in resource-limited settings, addressing technical adaptability, resource allocation, and local support infrastructure. The paper concludes by identifying current challenges and proposing future development directions intended to guide further research and implementation of infectious disease point-of-care diagnostics.
items.citation: Zhang YX, Ru JF. Point-of-care testing (POCT) for Infectious diseases: technological innovation, effectiveness evaluation, and application strategies in resource-limited regions.. Diagnostic microbiology and infectious disease. 2026

items.title: Finger-actuated microfluidic device for point-of-care circulating cell-free nucleic acid extraction.
items.summary: This paper describes the development and validation of a fully finger-actuated microfluidic device designed to extract cell-free nucleic acids from plasma without requiring external power or laboratory instrumentation. The device integrates finger-operated valves, a pump, and on-board blister reagent storage to carry out a complete sample-to-eluate workflow—including lysis, binding, washing, and elution—through simple manual actuation. Performance was benchmarked against commercial benchtop and automated robotic extraction workflows using DNA-spiked aqueous samples and human pooled plasma, with the device achieving recoveries comparable to or exceeding those of the benchtop method, particularly at lower input plasma volumes. Clinical utility was demonstrated using patient samples positive for cytomegalovirus, monkeypox virus, and chikungunya virus, with quantitative PCR cycle threshold values closely matching those from standard protocols. The authors propose that this instrument-free extraction tool could serve as a practical bridge between lateral flow amplification technologies and decentralised molecular diagnostics in resource-limited settings.
items.citation: Musaddaq G, Ehsan L, Yoga Y et al.. Finger-actuated microfluidic device for point-of-care circulating cell-free nucleic acid extraction.. Lab on a chip. 2026

items.title: EULAR recommendations for the management of rheumatoid arthritis with synthetic and biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs: 2025 update
items.summary: These updated recommendations address the management of rheumatoid arthritis using synthetic and biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, incorporating the most recent evidence on their efficacy and safety. An international task force conducted systematic literature reviews and applied a structured voting process to revise and consolidate guidance from the previous iteration. The resulting framework comprises five overarching principles and a reduced set of recommendations covering conventional synthetic agents, glucocorticoids, biologic drugs, and targeted synthetic drugs including Janus kinase inhibitors. The recommendations endorse methotrexate ideally combined with short-term glucocorticoids as initial therapy, with addition of a biologic agent advised upon insufficient response, while Janus kinase inhibitors remain an option subject to careful risk assessment for cardiovascular events, malignancies, and thromboembolic events. Tapering of therapy is supported in sustained remission but is approached cautiously given the frequent risk of disease flare upon cessation.
items.citation: Josef S. Smolen, Christopher J. Edwards, Victoria Konzett et al.. EULAR recommendations for the management of rheumatoid arthritis with synthetic and biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs: 2025 update. Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases. 2026

items.title: Smart wearable and implantable biosensors for continuous health monitoring: materials, biocompatibility, and AI integration
items.summary: This review examines the landscape of smart wearable and implantable biosensors designed for continuous, real-time monitoring of biophysical and biochemical signals in support of personalized and preventive healthcare. The authors survey advances in flexible, stretchable, and biocompatible materials that enable long-term comfort and stable body integration, alongside multimodal and multi-analyte sensing approaches that improve measurement robustness. The integration of artificial intelligence for signal processing and predictive health insights is also assessed as a key enabling strategy. Despite these advances, the review identifies persistent challenges including motion artifacts, energy autonomy, data privacy, and the clinical interpretability of sensor outputs. The paper synthesizes current progress across materials, device architectures, and AI-assisted strategies to outline the state of the field and its remaining obstacles.
items.citation: Thirumalaisamy Suryaprabha, Chunghyeon Choi, Yanfang Wu et al.. Smart wearable and implantable biosensors for continuous health monitoring: materials, biocompatibility, and AI integration. npj Flexible Electronics. 2026

items.title: Food and Medicine Homology Focus in 2026
items.summary: This perspective paper examines the anticipated trajectory of the food and medicine homology field as it transitions from traditional empirical knowledge toward evidence-based scientific frameworks. The authors outline a vision centered on expanding the recognized substance directory, establishing rigorous evidence standards, and deepening mechanistic understanding of active components through approaches such as gut microbiota research, phase separation, and immunometabolic reprogramming. Applications are expected to shift toward precision and dynamic health management by integrating multidimensional personal data with artificial intelligence to address chronic diseases and aging populations. The field is also anticipated to undergo industrial transformation through synthetic biology, intelligent delivery systems, and sustainable manufacturing to build a more transparent supply chain. Overall, the paper presents a forward-looking framework for how scientific rigor and technological innovation will reshape food and medicine homology research and practice around the year described.
items.citation: Mengyao Li, Gui-Fen Wu, Feng Lu et al.. Food and Medicine Homology Focus in 2026. Food & medicine homology.. 2026

items.title: Invisible Agents, Uninformed Patients: Towards Responsible Deployment Of Autonomous AI Diagnostic Agents In Sub-Saharan Africa
items.summary: This paper examines the deployment of autonomous AI diagnostic agents across eHealth platforms in sub-Saharan Africa, focusing on the accountability and consent challenges these systems create for patients in low-resource settings. The authors argue that existing frameworks for AI accountability, transparency, and explainability in healthcare are predominantly clinician-centered and assume regulatory conditions that do not reflect the realities of these contexts, leaving a structural accountability gap in which patients remain largely unaware that autonomous systems are influencing their diagnoses or triage decisions. Drawing on documented deployment cases from Tanzania, Zambia, and Ghana involving tuberculosis detection, diabetic retinopathy screening, and mobile health chatbot triage, the paper demonstrates that these gaps are not hypothetical but already present in active regional deployments. In response, the authors synthesize literature on informed consent, algorithmic accountability, and explainable AI to propose three foundational principles: agent-aware informed consent, mandatory human override capability, and contextually adapted explainability. These principles are offered as a practical minimum standard for developers, health administrators, and policymakers operating in environments where formal AI regulation remains nascent.
items.citation: Percy Brown, Kweku Yamoah. Invisible Agents, Uninformed Patients: Towards Responsible Deployment Of Autonomous AI Diagnostic Agents In Sub-Saharan Africa. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Time-Aware Tranformer-Based Prediction Model for AECOPD
items.summary: The paper addresses the challenge of predicting acute exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (AECOPD) in a timely manner, noting that conventional machine learning approaches relying on clinical and laboratory data introduce problematic delays. To overcome this limitation, the authors focused on home monitoring scenarios using only respiratory data collected from daily-use ventilators. They developed a Time-Aware transformer-based model that captures both the physiological symptoms and their temporal progression in ventilator data to generate informative patient representations. Experimental results showed that this approach outperformed traditional methods across multiple classification tasks, suggesting it could meaningfully improve the accuracy and timeliness of AECOPD prediction in real-world home settings.
items.citation: Weihao Qu, Ling Zheng, Dongyang Wang et al.. Time-Aware Tranformer-Based Prediction Model for AECOPD. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Beyond Fault Localization: A Trajectory-Level Study of LLM Agents for Microservice Root Cause Analysis
items.summary: This paper examined how large language model agents perform root cause analysis for microservice failures, arguing that existing evaluations are too narrow because they only check whether an agent correctly identifies the faulty service without assessing the quality of the diagnostic reasoning or fault-propagation reconstruction. The researchers developed a trajectory-level evaluation framework that compares agent diagnostic paths against manually curated fault-propagation routes, applying it to analyze thousands of diagnostic trajectories from a public benchmark. They found a systematic disconnect between answer correctness and diagnostic quality, identifying specific failure modes including omission of decisive evidence, misinterpretation of retrieved telemetry, and unsupported inference. Building on this taxonomy, they designed DiagGuard, a two-stage architecture that grounds diagnoses in available observations before localization and then audits the result against retrieved evidence, demonstrating meaningful improvement in localization accuracy on an independent benchmark. The work concludes that trajectory-level evaluation reveals important limitations hidden by final-answer metrics and offers concrete guidance for building more reliable automated diagnostic agents.
items.citation: Qisheng Lu, Aoyang Fang, Junjielong Xu et al.. Beyond Fault Localization: A Trajectory-Level Study of LLM Agents for Microservice Root Cause Analysis. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Fault Diagnosis of Dynamic Systems Under Unknown Operating Conditions: A Condition-Guided Selective Adaptation Approach
items.summary: The paper addresses the challenge of diagnosing faults in dynamic industrial systems when operating conditions during deployment are unknown and differ from those seen during training, a distribution shift that degrades model performance. The authors propose a condition-guided selective adaptation framework that combines an offline training phase, where continuous operating-condition adversarial learning with progressive training improves the model's generalization, with an online deployment phase that uses residual operating-condition responses to identify reliable unlabeled samples from streaming data for model updating. This two-stage design aims to adapt the diagnostic model to unseen conditions without requiring labeled data during deployment. Experiments on real-world gearbox and motor datasets show that the proposed approach achieves superior diagnostic accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods while keeping test-time computational costs relatively low.
items.citation: Jiaming Liu, Zeyi Liu, Hongshuo Zhao et al.. Fault Diagnosis of Dynamic Systems Under Unknown Operating Conditions: A Condition-Guided Selective Adaptation Approach. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Event-Time Confounding Under Bursty Human Dynamics
items.summary: This paper examines a systematic bias that arises when researchers study the effects of user-initiated digital events—such as opening an AI assistant or clicking a recommendation—by measuring activity afterward. The core problem identified is that such events tend to occur during ongoing task episodes, meaning that post-event activity surges may simply reflect the natural continuation of those episodes rather than any causal effect of the event itself. Using cross-surface web logs spanning AI, shopping, news, coding, and reference contexts, the authors demonstrate that activity rises broadly before such events and peaks prior to the moment of action, a pattern consistent with episode-selection bias rather than a genuine treatment effect. A particularly strong test employs known-null timestamps—markers that cause nothing—and shows that these null events still reproduce a substantial fraction of the excess post-event activity observed for real events, especially when users are already active. The authors formalize this bias, prove that single-surface event windows cannot disentangle it from genuine effects without additional assumptions, explain why common controls like user fixed effects and activity matching fail because the confound is within-user and time-varying, and offer a diagnostic protocol and open-source audit tool to help researchers identify and correct for the problem.
items.citation: Michael Iannelli, Alan Ai. Event-Time Confounding Under Bursty Human Dynamics. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Comprehensive Regression and Diagnostics for Non-Negative Data Using the BCSreg Package
items.summary: This paper introduces a software package for fitting flexible regression models to non-negative data that exhibit skewness, heavy tails, and potential point masses at zero — features that standard regression approaches handle poorly. The authors developed the BCSreg package for R, which implements Box-Cox symmetric and log-symmetric regression models for strictly positive continuous data, as well as zero-adjusted extensions for mixed discrete-continuous responses. The package allows simultaneous specification of regression structures for the scale parameter, relative dispersion, and the probability of zero occurrences through a unified formula interface, with parameters interpretable on the original data scale. It also provides a comprehensive suite of diagnostic tools, including randomized quantile residuals, simulated envelopes, and influence diagnostics tailored specifically to these model classes. The package's functionality is demonstrated through applications to real datasets.
items.citation: Francisco F. Queiroz, Rodrigo M. R. de Medeiros. Comprehensive Regression and Diagnostics for Non-Negative Data Using the BCSreg Package. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Author Correction: Cretaceous bird from Brazil informs the evolution of the avian skull and brain
items.summary: This paper is an author correction notice addressing an error in a previously published study on a Cretaceous bird from Brazil and avian skull and brain evolution. The original analysis of the enantiornithine bird *Navaornis hestiae* contained misplaced anatomical landmarks on its endocranial model, caused by a sharp corner in the three-dimensional reconstruction that displaced semilandmarks to an incorrect surface. The authors corrected the landmark positions using updated software and reanalyzed the dataset, producing a revised principal components analysis of endocranial shape variation. The core finding that *Navaornis* occupies an intermediate morphological position between stem birds and crown birds along the primary axis of shape variation is unchanged, though the corrected data now place *Navaornis* within crown bird variation along a secondary axis rather than just outside it. Additional shape distance analyses confirm that *Navaornis* shares endocranial similarities with a mix of stem and crown bird taxa, reinforcing the original interpretation of its mosaic of plesiomorphic and crown bird-like brain features.
items.why_notable: This work is drawing attention because it concerns a Cretaceous-era bird fossil from Brazil that provides new insights into how the avian skull and brain evolved, representing a significant paleontological find relevant to understanding early bird evolution.
